title: Determinant Quantum-Quantum Monte Carlo: Coherent Auxiliary-Field Sampling
authors: Xuepeng Wang, Sagnik Banerjee, Debanjan Chowdhury
abstract: We introduce determinant quantum-quantum Monte Carlo (DQ$^2$MC), a quantum algorithm that lifts the auxiliary-field sampling and averaging at the operational core of determinant quantum Monte Carlo onto a quantum computer. A determinant oracle synthesizes the DQMC amplitudes directly from a block encoding of the single-particle action matrix via quantum singular value transformations, so that the exponentially many Hubbard-Stratonovich weights are never enumerated, precomputed, or stored. Since the fermions are free for fixed auxiliary fields, the construction operates entirely at the single-particle level, requiring $O(\log N_{\mathrm{st}})$ system qubits and no Jordan-Wigner or Bravyi-Kitaev encoding, where $N_{\mathrm{st}}$ is the space-time volume. A full-quantum protocol makes observables interference amplitudes, eliminating the Markov chain and its autocorrelation time altogether; a hybrid quantum-classical protocol retains a constant-size active block of qubits and replaces the Metropolis-Hastings acceptance step with an exact heat-bath draw, so that cluster updates of any size are rejection-free, and passes only classical information between updates, admitting parallel tempering and distributed execution across quantum processors. The circuit-depth scales more favorably with spatial volume than classical DQMC, at the price of a post-selection overhead determined exactly by the largest target probability --- polynomial for smooth distributions, exponential for sharply peaked ones. Finally, the reweighting estimator underlying the fermion sign problem maps exactly onto a quantum weak value, placing the exponential cost of sign-problematic DQMC in precise correspondence with the post-selection overhead of weak-value extraction.
summary: This paper presents DQ2MC, a quantum algorithm designed to simulate strongly correlated electron systems by quantum mechanically implementing the sampling core of classical DQMC. It achieves this by synthesizing amplitudes directly from the action matrix, thus bypassing the exponential storage and sampling bottlenecks. The resulting hybrid protocol offers a path to quantum simulation that retains classical acceleration techniques while improving scaling over classical methods.
main_problem: The paper addresses the computational bottleneck in simulating strongly correlated lattice fermions, such as those found in the Hubbard model, where interactions are comparable to kinetic energy.
main_result: They introduce Determinant Quantum-Quantum Monte Carlo (DQ2MC), a quantum algorithm that lifts the auxiliary-field sampling onto a quantum computer, avoiding the enumeration of exponentially many weights.
method: The approach involves adapting the classical Determinant Quantum-Monte Carlo (DQMC) method by implementing its core sampling and averaging steps using quantum circuits, leading to both fully-quantum and hybrid quantum-classical protocols.
model_or_system: The focus is on strongly correlated lattice fermions, exemplified by the Hubbard model, relevant to high-temperature superconductivity and Mott insulators. The simulation relies on rewriting the partition function via the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation.
key_observables: Thermal expectation values of operators, such as the imaginary-time susceptibility $\chi_O(q, i\Omega_n)$.
important_parameters: The scaling is analyzed concerning the spatial volume ($N_{st}$), the imaginary time ($ eta$), and the overhead associated with the fermion sign problem.
main_assumptions: The hybrid protocol assumes that only classical information passes between quantum updates, and the full-quantum protocol assumes the one-body vertices can be implemented as controlled unitaries.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically compares classical DQMC (Markov chain) with DQ2MC (coherent superposition) and illustrates the measurement process using a Hadamard test estimator.
paper_structure: The paper reviews classical DQMC, then details the fully-quantum protocol (III), develops the hybrid quantum-classical protocol (IV), and discusses extensions.
why_interesting: The development of quantum algorithms for simulating interacting fermions directly impacts the field of quantum simulation, offering a potential quantum advantage over classical Monte Carlo methods for materials science.
